{{Short description|Set without nontrivial polynomial equalities}}
{{use mdy dates|date=September 2021}}
{{Use American English|date = January 2019}}
{{Ring theory sidebar}}
In [[abstract algebra]], a [[subset]] <math>S</math> of a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>L</math> is '''algebraically independent''' over a [[field (mathematics)#Subfields and prime fields|subfield]] <math>K</math> if the elements of <math>S</math> do not satisfy any non-[[trivial (mathematics)|trivial]] [[polynomial]] equation with coefficients in <math>K</math>.

In particular, a one element set <math>\{\alpha\}</math> is algebraically independent over <math>K</math> [[if and only if]] <math>\alpha</math> is [[Transcendental element|transcendental]] over <math>K</math>. In general, any element of an algebraically independent set <math>S</math> over <math>K</math> is by necessity transcendental over <math>K</math>, and over all of the [[field extension]]s of <math>K</math> generated by the remaining elements of <math>S</math>.

==Example==
The [[real number]]s <math>\sqrt{\pi}</math> and <math>2\pi+1</math> are [[transcendental number]]s: they are not the roots of any nontrivial polynomial whose coefficients are [[rational number]]s. Thus, the sets <math>\{\sqrt{\pi}\}</math> and <math>\{2\pi+1\}</math> are both algebraically independent over the rational numbers.

However, the set <math>\{ \sqrt{\pi}, 2\pi+1 \}</math> is ''not'' algebraically independent over the rational numbers <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>, because the nontrivial polynomial
:<math>P(x,y)=2x^2-y+1</math>
is zero when <math>x=\sqrt{\pi}</math> and <math>y=2\pi+1</math>.

==Algebraic independence of known constants==
Although [[Pi|{{pi}}]] and [[E (mathematical constant)|{{Math|{{var|e}}}}]] are transcendental, it is not known whether <math>\{ \pi , e \}</math> is algebraically independent over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>.<ref>{{cite book
| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=jQ7c8Xqpqk0C
| title = Field and Galois Theory
| author = Patrick Morandi
| publisher = Springer
| year = 1996
| pages = 174
| access-date = 2008-04-11
| isbn = 978-0-387-94753-2
}}</ref> In fact, it is not even known whether <math>\pi+e</math> is irrational.<ref>{{Citation |last=Green |first=Ben |author-link=Ben J. Green|chapter=III.41 Irrational and Transcendental Numbers |editor-last=Gowers |editor-first=Timothy |year=2008 |title=[[The Princeton Companion to Mathematics]] |page=222 |publisher=Princeton University Press}}</ref> [[Yuri Valentinovich Nesterenko|Nesterenko]] proved in 1996 that:
* the numbers <math>\pi</math>, <math>e^\pi</math>, and <math>\Gamma(1/4)</math>, where <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[gamma function]], are algebraically independent over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>.<ref name=MP61>{{cite book | first1=Yu. I. | last1=Manin | author-link1=Yuri I. Manin | first2=A. A. | last2=Panchishkin | title=Introduction to Modern Number Theory | series=Encyclopaedia of Mathematical Sciences | volume=49 | edition=Second | year=2007 | isbn=978-3-540-20364-3 | issn=0938-0396 | zbl=1079.11002 | page=61 }}</ref>
* the numbers <math>\pi, e^{\pi\sqrt{3}}</math>, and <math>\Gamma(1/3)</math> are algebraically independent over <math>\mathbb{Q}.</math>
* for all positive integers ''n'', the numbers <math>\pi</math> and <math>e^{\pi\sqrt{n}}</math> are algebraically independent over <math>\mathbb{Q}.</math><ref>{{cite journal|author=Nesterenko, Yuri V|author-link=Yuri Valentinovich Nesterenko|title=Modular Functions and Transcendence Problems|journal=[[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences|Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, Série I]]|volume=322|pages=909–914|year=1996|issue=10}}</ref>

==Results and open problems==
The [[Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem]] can often be used to prove that some sets are algebraically independent over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>. It states that whenever <math>\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n</math> are [[algebraic number]]s that are [[linearly independent]] over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>, then <math>e^{\alpha_1},\ldots,e^{\alpha_n}</math> are also algebraically independent over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>.

The [[Schanuel's conjecture|Schanuel conjecture]] would establish the algebraic independence of many numbers, including ''{{pi}}'' and {{Math|{{var|e}}}}'','' but remains unproven:

:Let <math>\{z_1,...,z_n\}</math> be any set of <math>n</math> [[complex numbers]] that are [[linearly independent]] over <math>\mathbb Q</math>. The [[field extension]] <math>\mathbb Q (z_1,...,z_n,e^{z_1},...,e^{z_n})</math> has [[transcendence degree]] at least <math>n</math> over <math>\mathbb Q</math>.

==Algebraic matroids==
{{main|Algebraic matroid}}

Given a [[field extension]] <math>L/K</math> that is not algebraic, [[Zorn's lemma]] can be used to show that there always exists a maximal algebraically independent subset of <math>L</math> over <math>K</math>. Further, all the maximal algebraically independent subsets have the same [[cardinality]], known as the [[transcendence degree]] of the extension.

For every [[finite set]] <math>S</math> of elements of <math>L</math>, the algebraically independent subsets of <math>S</math> satisfy the axioms that define the independent sets of a [[matroid]]. In this matroid, the rank of a set of elements is its transcendence degree, and the flat generated by a set <math>T</math> of elements is the intersection of <math>L</math> with the field <math>K[T]</math>. A matroid that can be generated in this way is called an '''algebraic matroid'''. No good characterization of algebraic matroids is known, but certain matroids are known to be non-algebraic; the smallest is the [[Vámos matroid]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Ingleton | first1 = A. W.
 | last2 = Main | first2 = R. A.
 | doi = 10.1112/blms/7.2.144
 | journal = [[Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society]]
 | mr = 0369110
 | pages = 144–146
 | title = Non-algebraic matroids exist
 | volume = 7
 | year = 1975| issue = 2
 }}.</ref>

Many finite matroids may be [[Matroid representation|represented]] by a [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] over a field <math>K</math>, in which the matroid elements correspond to matrix columns, and a set of elements is independent if the corresponding set of columns is [[linear independence|linearly independent]]. Every matroid with a linear representation of this type may also be represented as an algebraic matroid, by choosing an [[Indeterminate (variable)|indeterminate]] for each row of the matrix, and by using the matrix coefficients within each column to assign each matroid element a linear combination of these transcendentals. The converse is false: not every algebraic matroid has a linear representation.<ref>{{citation|title=Applied Discrete Structures|first=K. D.|last=Joshi|publisher=New Age International|year=1997|isbn=9788122408263|page=909|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lxIgGGJXacoC&pg=PA909}}.</ref>
